story_text:
## Meet Rainy 75 V2
## What's New
## Battery, 8K & Low Front
Keyboards make you choose. A big battery means a thick case. Speed means charging every few days. Lights mean a higher price. You pick one and give up the other.
We spent two years refusing to pick. V2 carries 10,000 mAh and still sits 17.4 mm low at the front. It reports 8,000 times a second when you want speed, and runs up to 1,000 hours when you would rather forget the cable. Every key lights up, and the price still starts at $99.
Big battery and low front. Fast and long-lived. Bright and $99. All of it, at once.
First the sound. Two switch housings: Thock, deep and round; Clack, bright and short. Pick one, or both if you want.
Then the feel. Three gasket mounts, soft, even and firm, that swap without tools.
Under all of it, foams, rebuilt: six layers instead of five, so what reaches your ear is the key and nothing else. You will do this for years. Every keystroke should be one you look forward to.
Hear the sound test:
256 keyboards in one case.
Three gasket mounts, six foam layers, two switches. That is 256 ways to build one keyboard, or 512 if you own both switches. One press opens the case, every switch is hot-swap, and nothing needs solder or a screwdriver. Finding your sound takes minutes, not a weekend.
Three gasket mounts. Swap them by hand.
One press and the case is open. No screws, no tools.
The top-right corner ships as two keys. Pull one, and the knob from the box takes its place. It sits in the same hot-swap socket a switch does.
Out of the box it is a volume dial. Press and hold, and the same dial sets the brightness of the keyboard's lights.
Then give it your own job. In WOBKEY Studio, turning left, turning right and pressing each take any key or shortcut you choose. Scroll a long page. Zoom a canvas. Scrub a timeline. Skip a track. Step back through undo. Whatever your hands do a hundred times a day, put it on the dial.
Want a screen instead? Pull both keys.
Hot-swap, like every switch on the board. Pull the keycap and the switch with the puller from the box. Press the encoder insto the same five-pin socket, set its cover on top, push the knob on.
The screens are easier still. Pull both keys and a screen module takes the whole corner. Magnets snap it into place. Pogo pins carry power and signal, so there is no cable to plug in. Two are available as add-ons: a color LCD that plays your own images and GIFs, and a dot-matrix display with its own knob that shows the pixel patterns you draw.
THE BACK IS YOURS TOO.
Turn V2 over. The rear panel is held by magnets. Press the button and it lifts off; set it back and it snaps home. No screws, no pry tool, no marks on the case.
Under it is a slot for the 2.4G receiver. The receiver travels inside the keyboard, so it can't fall out of your bag or stay behind on the desk.
And the panel is a canvas. Open our backplate tool in your browser, drop in a photo, pick your colorway, and see it on your keyboard before anything is printed. Download the print file, have it printed under glass, and snap it on.
## Design & Finish
'The fact is the sweetest dream that labor knows.'
— Robert Frost, Mowing
The dream was a $99 keyboard finished like a watch…
A world of care. In every grain.
The dream was a $99 keyboard finished like a watch. The fact is in your hands: a block of aluminum, milled; fine beads at 220-mesh, thousands a second, until the surface is one even satin, a grain the width of a hair, no tool mark left anywhere; a rear panel polished by hand. Run a fingertip along the case. Dreams are cheap. This one weighs 1,535 grams.
Five case colors, eight colorways, twelve SKUs: the same aluminum under every one, so the only decision left is the one you want to look at every day.

## In Stores
## Why This Price
This is the whole keyboard, taken apart and laid flat: the aluminum case, the plate, the circuit board, the foam, the batteries, every switch and every keycap. Nothing is hidden, and nothing here is filler. These parts cost us about $67 before anyone is paid to put them together. The bar shows where the rest of your $99 goes. Our share is the thin red slice at the end.
Say it plainly: we make money on this. Profit keeps us in the hobby we all joined for. Then the choice: the price that protects the brand, or the price more people can reach. We chose the people, and cut every cost we could find.
How the parts got this cheap: the $0.25 drink.
Last time, we told you: every glass raised at a supplier dinner took about a quarter off each keyboard. The factory asked us not to repeat it. We are. In 2026 everything costs more, so a glass buys about a nickel. We drank the same. The price stayed at $99. Thank you for keeping this way of life alive.
